A router is a consumer’s mouth and ears on the internet. What the consumer says to the internet comes out of the router’s mouth, and what the internet says back goes through the router’s ears. If compromised, the router can whisper lies in both directions, impersonating the consumer and creating a foothold in the consumer’s own home for state-sponsored cyberattacks. As the Federal Communications Commission has explained, “[c]ompromised routers can enable in-depth network surveillance, data exfiltration, botnet attacks, and unauthorized access to U.S. government or American businesses’ networks.”1 2.

Such activity not only puts a consumer’s internet connection at risk but also makes consumers involuntary participants in malicious campaigns carried out on behalf of foreign nations—something no Iowan consents to. That is the problematic activity TP-Link has exposed Iowans to through its misrepresentations and deceptive acts.

VIII. TP-Link’s Data Practices and Privacy Policies Deceive Consumers by Omitting the Risks from China’s Intelligence Laws

TP-Link’s mobile applications collect consumers’ personal data and claim to provide customization and control of their privacy and security settings, and its privacy policies reserve broad rights to share that data. But TP-Link fails to disclose a critical and material fact: TP-Link’s Chinese facilities, affiliates, and personnel are subject to PRC national intelligence laws mandating cooperation with PRC intelligence efforts, exposing American consumer data to potential PRC access. By omitting this material fact, TP-Link misleads consumers and fails to obtain informed consent regarding their data within its portfolio of networking and smart home device applications.

TP-Link offers applications such as TP-Link Tether, TP-Link Tapo, TP-Link Deco, and Kasa Smart on Apple’s App Store and Google’s Play Store. These applications can be required to operate TP-Link devices, are integral to set up and management of TP-Link services such as HomeShield, and grant consumers the ability to customize and control privacy and security settings. These apps are used with a wide range of TP-Link networking and smart home devices, such as cameras, fans, lights, and routers.83 89.

The Tether Privacy Policy states that TP-Link “may share your personal information internally and externally with suppliers, advisors, or partners for our legitimate business purposes, and only on a need-to-know basis.” It carves out the right to share information with “authorized partners, including affiliates . . . to: . . . comply with applicable laws,” and “where

TP-Link Knew Its Representations Were Misleading and Intended Iowans to Rely on Them

TP-Link sells security. It markets HomeShield as covering “all security scenarios,” advertises its routers by their “Cyber Security” and “Password Security,” and tells the public that “no government” controls the design and production of its devices. TP-Link makes those claims because it knows that security and foreign-government access matter to consumers deciding which router to buy, and it intends consumers to rely on them.

TP-Link also knew the facts it left out. It knew its routers were being conscripted into botnets: it said so itself in 2023, when it announced that the “AX21 has been added to the Mirai botnet Arsenal,” and again in January 2025, when it acknowledged that the Quad7 botnet is “predominantly TP-Link devices.” It knew where its research, development, and components come from. And it knew the laws of the country where that work is done. TP-Link omitted those facts with the intent that Iowa consumers would rely on its assurances of security and separation, and would buy its products, without them.
Claims Under the Consumer Fraud Act and Civil Penalties 102.
Under the Iowa Consumer Fraud Act:

The act, use or employment by a person of an unfair practice, deception, fraud, false pretense, false promise, or misrepresentation, or the concealment, suppression, or omission of a material fact with intent that others rely upon the concealment, suppression, or omission, in connection with the lease, sale, or advertisement of any merchandise or the solicitation of contributions for charitable purposes, whether or not a person has in fact been misled, deceived, or damaged, is an unlawful practice.

“Deception” means “an act or practice which has the tendency or capacity to mislead a substantial number of consumers as to a material fact or facts.” Iowa Code § 714.16(1)(c). An “unfair practice” is “an act or practice which causes substantial, unavoidable injury to consumers that is not outweighed by any consumer or competitive benefits.” Id. § 714.16(1)(i). The State need not show that any consumer was misled, deceived, or damaged. Id. § 714.16(2)(a).

TP-Link has engaged and continues to engage in the sale and advertisement of merchandise as defined in the Act to consumers throughout Iowa. Merchandise “includes any objects, wares, goods, commodities, intangibles, securities, bonds, debentures, stocks, real estate or services.” Id. § 714.16(1)(e).
TP-Link sells objects, wares, goods, intangibles, and services, including routers, networking devices, smart home devices, and related applications and services. 1.

The conduct described in the preceding paragraphs of this Petition constitutes “unfair practice, deception,” “misrepresentation,” and “concealment, suppression, or omission of . . . material fact with intent that others rely,” all unlawful practices under the Act. Id. § 714.16(2)(a). TP-Link has violated the CFA by, without limitation: a. Representing, expressly and by implication, that TP-Link devices are secure— including that HomeShield “covers all security scenarios,” “handles all your concerns,” and provides “preventions against any potential cyber threats or attacks,” and formerly that HomeShield provides a “100% safeguard”—despite security flaws and vulnerabilities; b. Making model-specific security representations—including that the TL-WR940N provides “[e]asy wireless security encryption” and “access control”; that the Archer C7 “provides secure Wi-Fi access for guests”; that the Archer AX21 offers “Refined Password Security” and a “New Level of Cyber Security”; and that the

Archer AXE75 has “advanced security features that deliver a safe environment”— when those models contained critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities; c. Making false or deceptive statements after vulnerabilities became public, including TP-Link’s April 2026 representation that all products affected by the Quad7 attacks had reached end-of-life status, which omitted the TL-WR940N until TP-Link corrected the omission in May 2026, with the intent that consumers rely on the omission; and d. Selling devices to Iowa consumers while failing to disclose material facts about repeated critical security vulnerabilities—including vulnerabilities exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers and the Russian GRU—and about default settings that do not support automatic firmware updates, leaving consumers unknowingly exposed, with the intent that consumers rely on the omission.

These facts are material. A router exists to move a household’s data safely between the home and the internet, and its security is the reason to choose one router over another. TP-Link knows this: it markets its routers by their security features and built HomeShield around that promise. A consumer deciding whether to put a TP-Link router at the center of the home network would want to know that the model had been conscripted into botnets run by Chinese and Russian intelligence services, and that TP-Link would stop patching it 108.

The unfair, false, misleading, and/or deceptive acts committed by Defendant to misrepresent and conceal the security of its devices constitute unlawful conduct under the CFA and have caused or are likely to cause substantial injury to Iowa consumers. Without an injunction from this Court, Defendant is likely to continue these practices, which would further harm Iowa consumers and the public.

Each instance of Defendant’s unfair and deceptive practices constitutes a separate violation of the Act. The State is entitled to civil penalties of up to $40,000 per violation of the Act under Iowa Code § 714.16(7).
